newsitem.title: FRANCE: France bails out Credit Lyonnais, seeks buyers.
newsitem.headline: France bails out Credit Lyonnais, seeks buyers.

text.p: The French government said Wednesday it would mount a third attempt to bail out Credit Lyonnais and declared it would consider offers for the ailing state-controlled bank.

"As of now, the government is ready to consider any proposals from investors for a minority or a majority stake," said the finance ministry, which originally planned to sell the bank by the year 2000.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told a news conference the new salvage operation would get the bank in shape to be sold after two previous rescue attempts -- in 1994 and 1995 -- had failed to ensure its recovery.
"We're embarking on a new era," he told reporters.

The latest rescue plan would be on top of 3.9 billion francs ($765 million) in emergency French aid appproved Wednesday by the European Commission, under which the government will assume costs imposed on the bank as part of last year's bailout.

The approval of the emergency package came just over a year after the European Commision cleared a 45 billion franc ($8.8 billion) state bailout of the bank, whose near collapse marked the biggest scandal in recent French banking history.
The accelerated timetable for the bank's sale was what the government gave in exchange for winning the European Commission's approval for fresh state aid, analysts said.

Arthuis said the sale of the bank, whose troubles stem from an expansion binge that briefly turned it into the world's biggest bank outside Japan, would take place "as quickly as possible" but was unlikely before year-end.
He said the government would be open to buyers from outside France for the bank, which was nationalised by President Charles de Gaulle following World War II.
Arthuis said the third rescue plan in the pipeline would be aimed at "ensuring its (the bank's) future and making it fully competitive."

He said the government would decide whether it needed to recapitalize Credit Lyonnais after the bank reported its first half results on Oct. 3. Some press reports have said that could cost 10 billion francs ($2 billion) or more.
Arthuis said the emergency help for the bank, which lost 21 billion francs ($4.1 billion) between 1992 and 1994, would come from other privatisation revenues.

The aid will cover the financing shortfall for a loan the bank was forced to extend at below market rates to a state-backed rescue vehicle that took over 130 billion francs ($25.5 billion) of its troubled assets last year.
The European Commission had insisted that the loan be made at below market rates in order to make Credit Lyonnais share in the cost of a reckless past.

But the bank had warned that the shortfall would plunge it back into the red. The emergency help is expected to allow the bank to post a modest profit when it announces its half-year results. It eked out a 13 million franc ($2.6 million) profit in 1995.
